title: What? An E-Bike?

body_markdown:
As Austin Powers said, “Honestly, it’s not mine. That’s just not my bag, baby.”


I mentioned a few weeks ago that my middle son Kyle (the one who lives in Santa Fe) is into vintage mopeds like I’m into vintage cars, but my oldest son Ethan (the one who lives with us) surprised us a few months back by coming home with a vintage Honda Hobbit gas moped, and rapidly followed that with a Juiced-brand E-bike. The snotty-loud Hobbit seemed like a purchase intended to ensure many brotherly texts and phone calls, but the E-bike appeared to be more practical—Ethan owned one a few years back and used it to commute to his former job. He parked it because he began working from home, and barely used it because it had no rear suspension and thus was uncomfortable. He sold it late this summer, and to our surprise, rapidly replaced it with this one with rear shocks.


The E-bike was a great buy for what it is, but it came with a few electrical quirks. The most pressing one was that the bike would suddenly lose all power, including to the display. Ethan read up on it on an enthusiast forum and learned that, not surprisingly, this was due to a bad connection between the beefy two-prong female connector on the battery pack and its male counterpart on the bike’s frame. The battery is held in place by a bracket on the bottom and a locking post that secures it at the top.


The E-bike’s removable battery.


Rob Siegel


The frame-mounted locking post and connector at the top.


Rob Siegel


People on the Juiced forum complain that the locking post develops play, and that, along with road vibration, creates movement in the pins of the connector that eventually results in pitting and burning. Ethan said he could hear the connector arcing as power disengaged and came back while he was riding. A visual inspection verified that the negative female pin in the socket was indeed damaged.


The smoking pin.


Rob Siegel


Ethan reported that the recommended solution on the forum was to do away with the round connectors entirely and replace them with XT60 side-by-side connectors that are commonly used for battery connections on a variety of devices. This made sense to me, as it decouples the mechanical mounting of the battery to the frame from the electrical connection.


A pair of XT60 connectors.


eBay


However, when the XT60 connectors arrived, I saw two issues. The first was that there didn’t seem to be enough clearance for the new connectors to sit between the battery and the frame, and the pigtails simply weren’t long enough to allow for them to be outside. The second was that the original round connectors had nice O-ring seals on them, whereas replacing that connector on the battery with a pair of wires passing through a grommet wouldn’t be nearly as good at keeping out the weather.


I asked Ethan to find more detailed info and/or pics on the forum where someone had actually done the conversion, and he couldn’t. As such, I recommended that he simply replace the connectors with new ones of the original style. He balked, saying that folks on the forum report failure after a thousand miles. My fatherly wisdom was, “A thousand miles on an E-bike sounds like a lot to me.” In the end, I convinced him that if the goal was to get the E-bike up and running, this was the easiest way to do it. New connectors arrived in a couple of days, and soldering the existing wires onto them was straightforward.


The battery pack needed to be opened up to change the connector. That’s a pair of larger XT90s connecting it to the lithium battery. I suppose we could’ve used a pair of XT90, but the clearance and weather-sealing issues would’ve remained.”


Rob Siegel


The replacement connector on the bike, all nicely soldered and heat-shrunk.


Rob Siegel


With the power problem solved, we could move on to the next issue, which was that the electric twist-throttle had obvious dead spots in it and would sometimes cut out completely while the rest of the bike still had power. The original throttle was no longer available, but a handlebar-compatible one with a similar-looking three-pin connector was. Ethan ordered it, but we immediately found that even though the connector pin face was the same, the attachment mechanism was different—the bike used little threaded metal rings that tightened around a rubber seal, and the new connector used a push-one-side-into-the-other, so they couldn’t mate. This meant needing to chop the connector off the bike and splice on another one, something I bristled at, as the wires were tiny and the splice would need to be made in the middle, not soldered onto the back as was the case with the battery connectors.


Original-style connector with knurled knobs on the bottom, new-style push-to-seal on the top.


Rob Siegel


I have a funny perspective on connector and wiring issues like this. On the one hand,[I wrote an automotive electrical book](https://www.amazon.com/dp/0837617510) , but on the other, I’m, well, me, and have done all sorts of unspeakable electrical things (I think that the taillights on my beautiful red BMW E9 coupe are still connected with speaker wire and twist-on wire nuts). I’ve gotten less hack-y as I’ve gotten older, but I’m still resolutely practical—if the goal is to make something work and save money, that’s fine.


But in this situation, I pushed back on Ethan. I *really* didn’t want to go cutting the head off a connector unless we were absolutely certain there was no other way. I thought that, since the throttle is just a resistance track, it could be cleaned with contact cleaner, but spraying it into the only groove available didn’t help, and I couldn’t find any way to open the thing up.


So, with that retreat exhausted, off with its head. Ethan installed the new throttle on the handlebars while I stripped wires. Before I began soldering things, I twisted red-to-red, black-to-black, and white-to-yellow, and we lifted up the rear wheel and twisted the throttle.


And… it didn’t work.


Assuming that, on anything like this, the three wires were 5V, ground, and signal, I tried all combinations with the voltmeter until I found which was which on the bike end (not surprisingly, red was 5V, black was ground, and white was signal). I asked Ethan to search online for the pinout diagram of the throttle he’d just bought, and it turned out that 5V and ground were reversed on the connector. We swapped red and black, did the wire-twist test again, and the raised rear wheel happily responded to the throttle.


That left soldering. A pack of[combined solder-band-and-heat-shrink connectors](https://www.amazon.com/Kuject-Connectors-Waterproof-Electrical-Automotive/dp/B073RMRCC3) came with the new throttle. These are the things where you just strip the insulation off the ends of both wires, insert them through the solder band, heat the thing with a heat gun, the solder band melts and joins the wires, and the heat shrink tubing seals the thing up. I use these in certain situations, but there are two caveats. The first is that I don’t think they’re ever going to make as solid and reliable a connection as when you tin the ends of both wires with solder, hook them over each other, squeeze them, then use a soldering iron to flow solder onto them. The second is that the size and stiffness of the connection they make can sometimes be bigger than it is if you solder and heat-shrink the wires yourself. So I did the latter.


Two down, one to go (this was before I squeezed the hooked ends together and flowed solder onto the joint.


Rob Siegel


The final task was to put a piece of heat-shrink over the entire repair. I made sure in advance that I could fit the tubing over the end of the connector. I left it to Ethan to do a bit of cable management with zip ties and secure the excess cable.


And done.


Rob Siegel


And with that, Ethan took the E-bike for two quick laps around the block. It worked flawlessly.


So, not a bad couple of wrenching sessions. I got to fix something that didn’t anger up my back and talk Ethan out of doing something I didn’t think was a good idea, and he got to experience some of my Hack Mechanic ethos where I say I don’t want to do it this way, walk down the path to doing it the other way, decide that it’s either worse or simply not possible, and reverse direction.


And hey, just because your kid is 38 doesn’t mean you can’t apply your fatherly skills to make him happy.


Kid and bike, both fully functional.


Rob Siegel


***
